title: The weaker brother (1 Corinthians 8)
hook: knowledge puffs up, love builds up
tomorrow: how can one man be 'all things to all men' and stay himself?

segments.voice: A week inside one letter: a trembling arrival, two gardeners, a temple of people, fools who bless, a body bought with a price, and yesterday, each has his gift.
screen: `EACH HAS HIS GIFT.` → `A WEEK INSIDE ONE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Win the argument, lose the friend: it happens at plenty of dinner tables. Corinth's next question is about dinner. Some meat in the city had been "offered unto idols." Can a believer eat it? One group has the answer ready: an idol is nothing, there's one God, meat is meat. Paul agrees with them on the facts. Then he says the facts aren't the end of it.
screen: `WIN THE ARGUMENT, LOSE THE FRIEND.` → `MEAT OFFERED UNTO IDOLS.` → `RIGHT, AND NOT DONE.`

segments.voice: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth." Charity, in the King James, is love. Knowledge inflates; love builds. Paul grants the theology: "we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one." But not everyone feels it in their bones. Someone who used to honor those idols sees a fellow believer eating in an idol's temple, and their tender conscience is pulled back toward what they left. So: "take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak." Then the line that names the day: "And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?" The weaker brother isn't a problem to fix. He's someone Christ died for. And Paul's own choice is blunt: "if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth". The whole week ran this way: a trembling man, a planter who isn't the point, fools who bless. Being right is half the question. The other half is what my freedom does to the person next to me.
screen: `AN IDOL IS NOTHING. AGREED.` · `KNOWLEDGE PUFFS UP.` · `ONE FOR WHOM CHRIST DIED.` · `I WILL EAT NO FLESH.` · then, large: `LOVE BUILDS UP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one freedom you have that someone near you struggles with: a drink, a kind of joke, a way of spending. Name the moment it might come up this week, and decide now what you'd set aside for them, quietly, without a speech.
The weaker brother. The one whose conscience is still tender, and who, Paul says, is someone Christ died for.
Hold onto this: love builds up, even when you're right and the facts are on your side. That's the week.

howItsDone: Christians turn to 1 Corinthians 8 when they think about freedom and conscience; some churches apply it to choices like drinking around someone who is struggling, and Christians weigh those choices differently.

fork.setup: your friend's family doesn't game on Sundays; your family does. he's at your house on a Sunday. what does 1 Corinthians 8 suggest?
options: pick something else to do, so his conscience isn't pushed.

fork.reveal: Paul grants the facts, then sets his freedom aside for the one whose conscience is tender: love builds up.

chat.says: last night here. pizza vote: pepperoni wins. hana doesn't eat pork. i could split a cheese one with her. lame?
options: Not lame. Pepperoni's allowed, but love builds up. Splitting one so she's not alone is the point.
Lame. You won the vote fair and square; she can order her own if she wants.
Skip pizza entirely so you don't make anyone uncomfortable. Being careful is safest.
chat.meaning: Paul agreed the meat was fine, then gave up his right for someone else's sake. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.

idols.meaning: statues worshiped as gods in the city's temples

charity.meaning: the King James word for love here
